performers: Philharmonic Symphony Orchestra of London; Artur Rodzinski, conductor
intro: Low strings fling a phrase at the violins, and the Fifth Symphony begins. Rodzinski conducts a movement that grows from that bare exchange to a brass-and-drum march, then ends with the small, cold gleam of a celesta.

sections.label: A · Low strings, high strings
sections.mNote: Cellos and basses exchange sharp phrases with the violins

sections.label: B · A long violin melody
sections.mNote: Harp and repeated lower strings support the quiet tune

sections.label: Dev · Piano in the bass
sections.mNote: Low piano figures and cellos set the development moving

sections.label: C · Brass and strings in force
sections.mNote: Brass chords and driven strings enlarge the opening argument

sections.label: B′ · Flute and horn
sections.mNote: The long melody returns above quiet repeated strings

sections.label: Coda · Violin, harp, then celesta
sections.mNote: Muted strings surround the last solos and celesta scales

cues.title: D minor in reply
cues.text: Cellos and basses leap from D to B♭; the violins answer. The phrases pull against one another across the orchestra, with rests leaving each reply exposed. Winds and brass wait.
cues.evidence: Shostakovich, Symphony No. 5, Muzgiz full score, plate M. 16313 Г, p. 3: Moderato, opening string exchange. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Pravda attacks the opera
cues.text: On 28 January 1936, Pravda prints an unsigned attack on Shostakovich’s Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District, headed “Muddle Instead of Music”. The opera is driven from Soviet theatres. More than a year later, in April 1937, Shostakovich begins the Fifth.
cues.evidence: Harlow Robinson, Boston Symphony Orchestra programme note, on the Pravda editorial, the opera’s ban and the Fifth begun on 18 April 1937: https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-5-shostakovich . The editorial itself, printed without a byline in Pravda, 28 January 1936 (Russian Wikisource transcription): https://ru.wikisource.org/wiki/%D0%A1%D1%83%D0%BC%D0%B1%D1%83%D1%80_%D0%B2%D0%BC%D0%B5%D1%81%D1%82%D0%BE_%D0%BC%D1%83%D0%B7%D1%8B%D0%BA%D0%B8

cues.title: Work begins on 18 April
cues.text: Shostakovich begins direct work on the symphony on 18 April 1937. He drafts the first three movements quickly; the finale and the full score take longer.
cues.evidence: DSCH Publishers, work history of Symphony No. 5 (editorial commentary): direct work began on 18 April 1937, with quick drafts of the first three movements; the finale and the full score took much longer. https://shostakovich-en.ru/140en Harlow Robinson (Boston Symphony note) also gives 18 April 1937 as the start and 20 July 1937 as the completion; the DSCH history has work continuing until at least 20 September, so no end date is given. https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-5-shostakovich

cues.title: A long violin line
cues.text: The violins stretch out a quiet melody over repeated notes in the lower strings. Harp chords mark the harmony beneath them. The tune has room to breathe, though the accompaniment keeps counting.
cues.evidence: Muzgiz full score, pp. 8–10, rehearsal 9 onwards: first violins marked pp espressivo, repeated lower strings and harp. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A first night in Leningrad
cues.text: On 21 November 1937, Yevgeny Mravinsky conducts the première in the Great Hall of the Leningrad Philharmonic. Shostakovich’s old teacher Maximilian Steinberg writes in his diary: “The ovation was stupendous.”
cues.evidence: DSCH Publishers, work history: première details and Steinberg’s diary entry after the concert of 21 November 1937. https://shostakovich-en.ru/140en

cues.title: The piano starts digging
cues.text: The piano enters low down, with short, hard-edged figures beside the cellos and basses. Horns stretch longer notes above it. The accompaniment has become the thing driving the music.
cues.evidence: Muzgiz full score, pp. 12–13, rehearsals 17–18: low piano, cellos and basses, followed by horns. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: No title, no dedication
cues.text: The Fifth has no dedication and no descriptive title, though Shostakovich liked titles. Harlow Robinson suggests that after the Lady Macbeth scandal he may have judged it safer to give his critics nothing to misread.
cues.evidence: Harlow Robinson, Boston Symphony Orchestra programme note on Symphony No. 5. https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-5-shostakovich

cues.title: Mravinsky lifts the score
cues.text: At the première, a listener remembers, the audience begins to rise from its seats one by one during the finale, until the whole hall is standing. Mravinsky holds the score high above his head. The artist Lyubov Yakovleva writes in her diary that everyone repeated the same thing: “he retaliated and retaliated well.”
cues.evidence: DSCH Publishers, work history of Symphony No. 5: the testimony of an unnamed contemporary (the audience rising “one by one” during the finale; Mravinsky raising the score above his head) and Lyubov Yakovleva’s diary entry after the concert of 21 November 1937 (“the ovation was rabid and demonstrative”; “he retaliated and retaliated well”), in the English page’s translation. https://shostakovich-en.ru/140en

cues.title: Brass over the marching strings
cues.text: Trumpets and trombones bear down on the strings. Repeated notes and heavy brass chords turn the movement into a march, with percussion adding its hard edge. The opening’s small exchanges have become orchestral proclamations.
cues.evidence: Muzgiz full score, pp. 34–36: brass chords, repeated string figures and percussion in the climactic development and return. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Flute beside a horn
cues.text: The lyrical tune returns in the flute and horn, over harp and gently repeated strings. A phrase that once belonged to the violin section is now passed between two solitary players.
cues.evidence: Muzgiz full score, p. 46, rehearsal 39: Più mosso, flute and horn solos over harp and quiet repeated strings. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A lyrical-heroic symphony
cues.text: In January 1938 Literaturnaya gazeta prints Shostakovich’s remark that his new work “could be called a lyrical-heroic symphony”. In the introduction to the 1956 score he gives its subject as “the shaping of the individual”: he saw “man with all his experiences” at the centre, in a work “lyrical in essence from start to finish”.
cues.evidence: DSCH Publishers, English page: “The subject of this symphony is the shaping of the individual. I saw man with all his experiences as central to the idea behind this work, which is lyrical in essence from start to finish”, from Shostakovich’s introduction to the score (Muzgiz, 1956). https://shostakovich-en.ru/140en Russian page, with the 1938 statement «Мое новое произведение можно назвать лирико-героической симфонией» (source given as “Пятая симфония Шостаковича”, Literaturnaya gazeta, 12 January 1938; our translation). https://shostakovich.ru/140ru Harlow Robinson’s Boston Symphony note quotes the two statements together in a looser translation (“genesis of the individual”, “man and all his sufferings”); the Russian «переживания» means experiences, so his wording is not used. https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-5-shostakovich

cues.title: A celesta at the edge
cues.text: The coda pares the orchestra down to solo violin, harp and muted strings. On the last page, the celesta climbs in small, bright scales while the bass and inner strings die away.
cues.evidence: Muzgiz full score, pp. 50–51, rehearsals 44–47: muted strings, solo violin, harp and closing celesta scales; final parts marked morendo. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A long tune above repeated strings
transitions.how: The winds withdraw and the strings become very quiet. Harp chords and repeated notes in the lower strings establish a steady accompaniment; above them the first violins begin their long melody, marked pp espressivo.
transitions.evidence: Muzgiz full score, pp. 8–10, rehearsal 9 onwards. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf

transitions.title: The piano takes over the bass
transitions.how: The harp’s sustained chords finish, the violin line sinks away, and the low piano begins its clipped figures. Cellos and double basses join it; the horns then lay a slower phrase over the moving bass. The piano is marked una corda, using the soft pedal.

transitions.title: The flute resumes the long melody
transitions.from: C · Brass and strings in force
transitions.how: A slowing passage ends with the brass dying away. At Più mosso, harp chords and repeated strings return very softly. Flute and horn share the lyrical melody above them; the heavy orchestral bass has fallen silent.

transitions.title: Muted strings surround the final solos
transitions.how: The score returns to Moderato, now at crotchet = 42. Muted violas, cellos and basses carry the opening rhythm beneath a flute solo. Harp and solo violin follow; the celesta’s ascending scales belong to the last page.

Long violin line over patterned lower strings and harp, pp. 8–10/rehearsal 9 and following; proportional placement within the quieter B span, supported by the report’s sustained low levels after 3:15.
Low-register development texture, pp. 12–13; report boundaries at 5:10/5:22 support the regional marker, not an exact horn entrance.

Reduced flute-and-horn lyrical texture, p. 46/rehearsal 39; approximately after the measured withdrawal near 11:00.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Philharmonic Symphony Orchestra of London (orchestra), Artur Rodzinski (conductor)
fields.note: Original sleeve and labels establish the displayed credit. Later Westminster reissue documentation and the publisher’s discography identify the orchestra as the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra. That cross-identification is not substituted silently for the original label credit; individual players and soloists are not established.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The work and movement are identified, but the exact performing edition is not. The historical score supports broad orchestration and formal observations, not a claim of bar-exact agreement with Rodzinski’s materials. The movement is the entire supplied source track; no local audio edit is made. The set’s finale has a separately disclosed reported cut.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: CiNii’s record for Westminster MVCW-18008 explicitly gives this range; the publisher independently lists the Rodzinski/Royal Philharmonic recording as 1954. Applying those reissue data to this differently credited LP is an inference. No original session ledger or precise movement-by-movement day has been located. 1956 is the selected LP’s publication year, not an invented session date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Venue transcribed exactly from the reissue catalogue record. The original LP does not supply a venue. Its linkage to the selected LP is the same qualified inference as the session-date attribution; no more specific hall name is invented.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Original sleeve and labels; commercially issued Vinyl LP, Made in U.S.A. Sleeve ©1956 Westminster Recording Sales Corp.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: Both forms are visually present on the source object. These identify the selected 1956 issue, not an asserted first edition worldwide. The publisher lists an earlier 1955 Nixa issue of the attributed 1954 performance.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Side 1: XTV 22720; movement 1 on that side
fields.note: Label matrix is legible in the scan. Side 1 contains Moderato/Allegretto; side 2 contains Largo/Allegro non troppo. Take numbers and faint runout/stamper suffixes are unknown and are not guessed.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The explicit ripping_operator field is credited, not the different uploader/cataloguing operator. A separately named restoration engineer and original recording engineer are unknown.

fields.label: Transfer date

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: LP transfer: Technics SL1200MK5 / Audio-Technica AT95e → Radio Design Labs EZ-PH1 → Focusrite Scarlett 2i2; ArchiveCD 2.2.57lp; source-side 24-bit FLAC and Internet Archive VBR MP3 derivatives
fields.note: Hardware lineage and ripping software are explicit metadata. Original side FLAC tags say Processed by SoX; exact filtering, declicking, gain, speed calibration and derivative segmentation parameters are unknown. The sleeve’s Panorthophonic tape-recording and RIAA-mastering statements concern the original production, not a modern restoration recipe. No local speed correction, normalization, splice or replacement audio was applied.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Not cleared as public domain in the EU or US; composition rights remain separate from the historic recording basis
fields.note: Shostakovich died in 1975. The ordinary EU life-plus-70 calculation runs through 2045; this is not a global clearance or a statement of a US expiry date. IMSLP identifies the work as non-public-domain in the EU and US. The inspected score is territorially hosted as public domain in Taiwan and is cited, not republished. No composition licence is asserted.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3: territorial EU historic-recording basis; commercial circulation documented by December 1955, selected LP issue dated 1956
fields.note: The original Westminster sleeve/labels and album metadata establish the selected 1956 WN 18001/XWN 18001 issue. A visually inspected High Fidelity review, December 1955, p. 80, already names this London orchestra, Rodzinski, his second recording of the Fifth and Westminster catalogue 18001; the review prints SWN 18001 and erroneously calls the symphony D major, so those details are not silently normalized. The publisher also lists Nixa WLP 20004 in 1955. First lawful publication anywhere before 1963 is the rule; no EU-first-release claim is required or made. source.rights.published 1956 remains a conservative upper bound tied to the selected physical issue, not a first-release date. Even using 1956, the ordinary 50-year recording term had expired before the 2013 extension. US sound-recording status is not established. Complete item metadata, original side-transfer provenance and scans disclose no Creative Commons non-commercial condition or separate upstream digital source. This is not a worldwide public-domain or composition-rights clearance.

sources.title: Symphony No. 5 — inspected historical full score
sources.locator: Printed pp. 3–51; PDF pp. 5–53. 170-page PDF; printed pages are PDF page minus two. Relevant pages were visually inspected for orchestration. This source is a historical score witness, not proof of the exact performing edition or a bar-aligned transcript of the cut finale.

sources.title: Niek Nelissen — Artur Rodzinski, Complete Westminster Recordings
sources.locator: OpusKlassiek, August 2026, Eloquence 484 8489 review. Early paragraph specifies a 37-bar cut in the 1942 Fifth finale; the later Westminster paragraph explicitly states that Rodzinski made the same cut. This supports a reported version difference, not the exact omitted bars or the splice time in this transfer.

sources.title: Museum collection — Pravda, “Muddle Instead of Music,” 28 January 1936
sources.locator: Catalogue of the surviving printed clipping of “Сумбур вместо музыки,” Pravda, 28 January 1936, inventory КП 317996/1315. Establishes the dated public attack, not a decoded political programme for individual notes.

sources.title: Harlow Robinson — Boston Symphony Orchestra work note
sources.locator: Used for Shostakovich’s dates (1906–1975) and the first American performance, Rodzinski/NBC Symphony broadcast, 9 April 1938. The note’s broader interpretive narrative is not treated as proof of private intentions.

sources.title: Testimony — publication and authenticity controversy
sources.locator: 1979 publication by Solomon Volkov, and summary/bibliography of the authenticity dispute, including Laurel Fay. Used only to identify the disputed status of the memoir claim, not as authentication of a Shostakovich quotation.

sources.title: Alex Ross — Unauthorized
sources.locator: The New Yorker, 30 August 2004 / 6 September print issue. Reports Testimony’s 1979 publication, Laurel Fay’s documentary challenge and the continuing distinction between corroborated anecdotes and authenticated authorship. Used as independent evidence of the controversy, not as a settled verdict on every memoir statement or on the finale’s meaning.

composer.epithet: He wrote fifteen symphonies under Soviet rule and signed some of his most personal music with four notes: D–E♭–C–B.
facts: Petrograd Conservatory, 1919–25; Nikolayev for piano, Steinberg for composition
Leningrad from 1937; Moscow from 1943; both posts lost in 1948
D–E♭–C–B♮: DSCH in German note names
Fifteen symphonies and fifteen quartets; operas, concertos and cinema scores
composer.background:
For five weeks the cinema had been showing the same film, and Shostakovich had been playing the same accompaniment. “I’ve even started dreaming about this music,” he wrote from Leningrad to Boleslav Yavorsky on 18 October 1925. He was nineteen. His First Symphony was finished, but a graduation score did not pay the household bills. His father had died three years earlier; accompanying silent films helped keep the family going.

He had been born in St Petersburg in 1906 and learnt the piano from his mother, Sofiya. At the Petrograd Conservatory, which he entered in 1919, Leonid Nikolayev taught him piano and Maximilian Steinberg composition. Alexander Glazunov, the director, recognised his gifts and helped him through his student years. He graduated as a pianist in 1923 and as a composer in 1925.
